tool.name: OpenAPI
tool.tagline: Machine-readable descriptions of HTTP APIs for docs, codegen and testing
tool.description: The OpenAPI Specification is a standard, language-agnostic format (YAML or JSON) for describing HTTP APIs: their paths, parameters, request and response bodies, and security. From one OpenAPI document teams generate interactive documentation, client SDKs and server stubs, mock servers, and contract tests, making it the backbone of API-first development.

concepts.name: What OpenAPI is for
concepts.summary: An OpenAPI document is a machine-readable contract for an HTTP API that drives docs, client generation, mocks and tests.
concepts.why: One accurate description replaces hand-written docs, SDKs and guesswork about an API.
concepts.body:
The **OpenAPI Specification (OAS)** defines a standard way to describe an HTTP API in YAML or JSON: which **paths** exist, which **operations** (GET, POST...) they support, their **parameters**, **request bodies**, **responses**, and **security** requirements. The document is readable by humans and by tools.

What teams do with it:

- **Documentation**: Swagger UI, Redoc, Scalar and others render interactive reference docs with "try it" consoles.
- **Code generation**: typed client SDKs and server stubs in dozens of languages.
- **Mocking**: serve realistic fake responses before the backend exists.
- **Validation and testing**: check requests and responses against the contract, lint for consistency, detect breaking changes in CI.
- **Gateways and AI agents** import OpenAPI to configure routes or call APIs as tools.

Some history: OpenAPI began as **Swagger** 2.0 and was donated to the Linux Foundation's OpenAPI Initiative in 2015. "Swagger" now names SmartBear's tools. Version **3.0** (2017) restructured the format; **3.1** (2021) aligned schemas fully with JSON Schema 2020-12 and added webhooks; **3.2** (2025) is backwards compatible with 3.1 and adds features such as hierarchical tags, the QUERY method and streaming media types.

Two workflows exist: **design-first** (write the document, then implement) and **code-first** (generate the document from annotated code, as FastAPI or Spring do). Both work if the document stays the source of truth that is tested.
concepts.code:
# The smallest useful OpenAPI document
openapi: 3.1.1
info:
  title: Todo API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /todos:
    get:
      summary: List todos
      responses:
        '200':
          description: The todos
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    id: { type: integer }
                    title: { type: string }
takeaways: OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs in YAML or JSON
One document drives docs, SDKs, mocks and tests
Swagger 2.0 became OpenAPI 3.x; Swagger now names tools
Design-first or code-first, keep the document as the contract
pitfalls: Treating the document as one-off documentation that drifts from the real API.

options: A family of tools; the spec is called OpenAPI
quiz.explain: Swagger 2.0 was renamed OpenAPI when donated; Swagger UI and Editor are tools.

concepts.name: Document structure
concepts.summary: Know the top-level fields of an OpenAPI document: openapi, info, servers, paths, components, security and tags.
concepts.why: Everything you write later lives in one of these few sections.
concepts.body:
An OpenAPI document is one object (YAML is most common; JSON is equivalent). Its top-level fields:

- `openapi` (required): the spec version, e.g. `3.1.1`. Tools use it to choose parsing rules.
- `info` (required): `title`, `version` (of **your API**, not the spec), plus optional `description` (Markdown), `contact`, `license`.
- `servers`: base URLs such as `https://api.example.com/v1`. Paths are appended to them; server variables allow templating like `https://{region}.api.example.com`.
- `paths`: the endpoints and their operations. In 3.1 a document may have no paths at all, for example when it only defines webhooks or shared components.
- `components`: reusable schemas, parameters, responses, request bodies, examples, headers and security schemes.
- `security`: the default security requirement for all operations.
- `tags`: groups for operations, with descriptions shown in docs.
- `webhooks` (3.1+): requests your API sends to subscribers.

Any object can carry **specification extensions**, fields starting with `x-` (`x-internal: true`), which tools may interpret.

Large APIs are split across files and joined with `$ref` to relative files (`$ref: './schemas/user.yaml'`). Bundlers like `redocly bundle` produce a single file for tools that need one.
concepts.code:
openapi: 3.1.1
info:
  title: Bookstore API
  version: 2.3.0                # version of YOUR API
  description: Manage books and orders.
  contact: { email: api@example.com }
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v2
    description: Production
  - url: https://{region}.sandbox.example.com/v2
    variables:
      region: { default: eu, enum: [eu, us] }
tags:
  - name: books
    description: Catalogue operations
security:
  - bearerAuth: []
paths: {}                       # operations go here
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer }
takeaways: `openapi` = spec version; `info.version` = your API's version
Paths are appended to `servers` URLs
`components` holds everything reusable
`x-` fields are extensions for tools
pitfalls: Putting the spec version in `info.version` or vice versa.

options: The version of the described API
quiz.explain: The `openapi` field holds the spec version; `info.version` is your API's own version.

concepts.name: Paths, operations and parameters
concepts.summary: Describe endpoints with path templates, operations with operationIds and tags, and path, query, header and cookie parameters.
concepts.why: Paths and parameters are the bulk of every API description.
concepts.body:
Each key under `paths` is a **path template** relative to the server URL, with variables in braces: `/books/{bookId}`. Under it, keys are HTTP methods (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`...), each an **operation object**.

Useful operation fields:

- `operationId`: a unique name like `getBook`. Code generators use it as the method name, so pick stable, descriptive ids.
- `summary` and `description` for docs; `tags` to group operations.
- `parameters`, `requestBody`, `responses`, `security`, `deprecated: true`.

**Parameters** have a `name`, an `in` location and a `schema`:

- `in: path`: part of the URL template. Path parameters must always be `required: true`.
- `in: query`: `?limit=20`. Arrays and objects are serialized according to `style` and `explode` (default for query: `form`, exploded, so `?tag=a&tag=b`).
- `in: header`: custom headers such as `X-Request-Id`. Do not describe `Accept`, `Content-Type` or `Authorization` as parameters; they are covered by `content` and security schemes.
- `in: cookie`.

Parameters shared by all operations of a path can be listed at the path level. Each operation's parameters are identified by `name` plus `in`.

Path templates must not overlap ambiguously: `/books/{id}` and `/books/{isbn}` are the same template and invalid together.
concepts.code:
paths:
  /books/{bookId}:
    parameters:
      - name: bookId
        in: path
        required: true            # always required for path params
        schema: { type: string }
    get:
      operationId: getBook
      tags: [books]
      summary: Get one book
      parameters:
        - name: include
          in: query
          schema:
            type: array
            items: { type: string, enum: [author, reviews] }
          # serialized as ?include=author&include=reviews
        - name: X-Request-Id
          in: header
          schema: { type: string, format: uuid }
      responses:
        '200': { description: The book }
        '404': { description: No such book }
takeaways: Path templates use `{name}`; path params are always required
operationId becomes the method name in generated SDKs
Parameters live in path, query, header or cookie
Don't model Content-Type, Accept or Authorization as parameters
pitfalls: Forgetting `required: true` on a path parameter, which makes the document invalid.

quiz.q: Why does `operationId` deserve a carefully chosen, stable name?
options: It is shown as the HTTP status
Code generators use it as the SDK method name
quiz.explain: Changing it renames methods in every generated client.

concepts.name: Request bodies and responses
concepts.summary: Describe request and response payloads by media type, list responses by status code, and document headers and examples.
concepts.why: Clients care most about exactly what they send and get back.
concepts.body:
A **request body** is described with `requestBody`, keyed by **media type** under `content`:

```yaml
requestBody:
  required: true
  content:
    application/json:
      schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/NewBook' }
```

Several media types can be offered (`application/json`, `multipart/form-data`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`). Request bodies are optional unless `required: true`.

**Responses** are keyed by HTTP status code (quoted strings in YAML: `'200'`), by range (`'4XX'`), or `default` for everything else. Each response must have a `description` and may have `content` and `headers`:

- Document every status a client should handle: success, `400` validation errors, `401`/`403`, `404`, `409`, `429`.
- Use `default` for a shared error format, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details (`application/problem+json`).
- Responses without a body (e.g. `204`) simply omit `content`.
- Response `headers` cover things like `Location` after a `201` or `Retry-After` on `429`.

**Examples** make docs and mocks realistic. Use `example` inside a schema, or named `examples` on a media type (each with `summary` and `value`). Mock servers and docs pick them up.
concepts.code:
paths:
  /books:
    post:
      operationId: createBook
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [title, isbn]
              properties: { title: { type: string }, isbn: { type: string, pattern: '^\d{13}$' } }
            examples:
              novel: { summary: A novel, value: { title: Kindred, isbn: '9780807083697' } }
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Created
          headers:
            Location: { schema: { type: string, format: uri } }
        '400':
          description: Validation failed
          content:
            application/problem+json:
              schema: { type: object, properties: { title: { type: string }, detail: { type: string } } }
takeaways: Bodies are described per media type under `content`
Responses keyed by status code (quoted), range or `default`
Every response needs a `description`
Named `examples` feed docs and mock servers
pitfalls: Documenting only the 200 response, leaving clients to discover error formats in production.

quiz.q: How do you describe a 204 No Content response?
options: A response with a description and no `content`
quiz.explain: Simply omit `content`; the description is still required.

concepts.name: Schemas with JSON Schema
concepts.summary: Model data with OpenAPI 3.1 schemas: types, required, formats, enums, nullability via type arrays, and constraints.
concepts.why: Schemas drive validation, generated types and docs, so precision pays off everywhere.
concepts.body:
In OpenAPI 3.1, the **Schema Object** is a superset of **JSON Schema 2020-12**, so any JSON Schema knowledge applies directly.

Core keywords:

- `type`: `string`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `array`, `object`, `null`.
- `properties` and `required` (a list at the object level, not a flag on each property).
- `additionalProperties`: `false` to forbid unknown fields, or a schema for map-like objects.
- `items` for arrays, plus `minItems`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems`.
- String constraints: `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, and `format` (`date-time`, `email`, `uuid`, `uri`). Formats are annotations by default; validators may or may not enforce them.
- Numbers: `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `multipleOf`.
- `enum` and `const`; `default`; `readOnly` (in responses only, like `id`) and `writeOnly` (in requests only, like `password`).

**Nullability changed in 3.1**: write `type: [string, 'null']`. The 3.0 keyword `nullable: true` no longer exists. Also, 3.0's `example` in schemas gives way to JSON Schema `examples` (an array).

Tips: a property not listed in `required` is optional, which is different from nullable. Use `integer` with `format: int64` for 64-bit ids, and remember some JavaScript clients lose precision above 2^53; many APIs send such ids as strings.
takeaways: 3.1 schemas are JSON Schema 2020-12
`required` is a list on the object; optional differs from nullable
Nullable in 3.1: `type: [string, 'null']`
readOnly for server-set fields, writeOnly for secrets
pitfalls: Using `nullable: true` in a 3.1 document; it is silently ignored or rejected by tools.

quiz.q: How is a nullable string written in OpenAPI 3.1?
quiz.explain: 3.1 follows JSON Schema, where null is a type that can appear in a type array.

concepts.name: Components and $ref
concepts.summary: Define schemas, parameters, responses and examples once under components and reference them with $ref, across files too.
concepts.why: Reuse keeps large API descriptions consistent and generates cleaner SDK types.
concepts.body:
Anything you repeat belongs in `components`, in the section for its kind: `schemas`, `parameters`, `responses`, `requestBodies`, `headers`, `examples`, `securitySchemes`, `links`, `callbacks`, and (3.1) `pathItems`.

Reference it with a **JSON Reference**: `$ref: '#/components/schemas/Book'`. The part after `#` is a JSON Pointer into the document. References can point to other files too: `$ref: './schemas/book.yaml'` or `'common.yaml#/components/responses/NotFound'`.

Good reuse patterns:

- Named schemas for every domain object. Generators turn each into a named class or type; inline anonymous schemas become awkward names like `InlineResponse2001`.
- Shared parameters (`Limit`, `Cursor`) and shared error responses (`NotFound`, `ValidationError`).
- Separate input and output shapes when they differ (`NewBook` vs `Book`), or rely on `readOnly`/`writeOnly`.

`$ref` semantics: in 3.0, a `$ref` object replaces the whole object, so sibling keywords are ignored. In 3.1, inside schemas `$ref` behaves like JSON Schema and siblings are allowed (e.g. a `description` next to `$ref`); Reference Objects elsewhere may only add `summary` and `description`.

Keep the tree navigable: split by domain (`schemas/`, `paths/`) for big APIs, and bundle into a single file for publishing.
concepts.code:
paths:
  /books:
    get:
      operationId: listBooks
      parameters:
        - $ref: '#/components/parameters/Limit'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A page of books
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: { type: array, items: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Book' } }
        '400': { $ref: '#/components/responses/ValidationError' }
components:
  parameters:
    Limit: { name: limit, in: query, schema: { type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 100, default: 20 } }
  responses:
    ValidationError:
      description: The request is invalid
      content:
        application/problem+json:
          schema: { $ref: './schemas/problem.yaml' }   # another file
  schemas:
    Book: { $ref: './schemas/book.yaml' }
takeaways: Put repeated schemas, parameters and responses in components
`$ref` is a JSON Pointer, locally or into other files
Named schemas become clean SDK types
3.1 allows siblings next to `$ref` inside schemas
pitfalls: Inlining the same schema in many places so it drifts and generates many duplicate types.

options: A JSON Pointer into the current document
quiz.explain: The fragment after # is a JSON Pointer path inside the document.

concepts.name: Security schemes
concepts.summary: Declare API keys, HTTP bearer and basic auth, OAuth 2.0 flows and OpenID Connect, and apply them globally or per operation.
concepts.why: Docs consoles, SDKs and gateways all need to know how to authenticate.
concepts.body:
Authentication is described in two steps: **define** schemes under `components.securitySchemes`, then **require** them with `security`.

Scheme types:

- `apiKey`: a key in a header, query parameter or cookie (`in: header`, `name: X-API-Key`).
- `http`: standard HTTP auth with `scheme: bearer` (optionally `bearerFormat: JWT`) or `scheme: basic`.
- `oauth2`: one or more `flows` (`authorizationCode`, `clientCredentials`, `deviceAuthorization` in 3.2) with URLs and the available **scopes**.
- `openIdConnect`: an `openIdConnectUrl` pointing at the provider's discovery document.
- `mutualTLS` (3.1+).

A **security requirement** is a map of scheme names to required scopes: `- oauth: [books.read]`. Semantics to get right:

- Entries in the `security` **list** are alternatives (OR).
- Several schemes in **one** entry must all be satisfied (AND).
- Top-level `security` applies to every operation; an operation-level `security` replaces it. `security: []` marks an operation as public, and `- {}` inside the list makes authentication optional.

Security schemes only describe what the API expects; they do not enforce anything. Never put real credentials in the document or its examples.
concepts.code:
components:
  securitySchemes:
    apiKey: { type: apiKey, in: header, name: X-API-Key }
    oauth:
      type: oauth2
      flows:
        authorizationCode:
          authorizationUrl: https://auth.example.com/authorize
          tokenUrl: https://auth.example.com/token
          scopes:
            books.read: Read the catalogue
            books.write: Change the catalogue
security:                      # default: OAuth OR API key
  - oauth: [books.read]
  - apiKey: []
paths:
  /health:
    get:
      security: []             # public endpoint
      responses: { '200': { description: OK } }
  /books:
    post:
      security:
        - oauth: [books.write] # overrides the default
      responses: { '201': { description: Created } }
takeaways: Define schemes in components, require them with `security`
List entries are OR; schemes within one entry are AND
Operation `security` overrides the global one; `[]` = public
OAuth scopes are declared on the scheme and required per operation
pitfalls: Listing two schemes as separate entries when the API actually needs both (AND).

options: Either an API key or an OAuth token with `read`
Both an API key and an OAuth token

concepts.name: Polymorphism: oneOf, anyOf, allOf, discriminator
concepts.summary: Compose schemas with allOf, describe alternatives with oneOf and anyOf, and help tools pick the right type with a discriminator.
concepts.why: Real payloads have variants, and how you model them decides whether SDKs get usable types.
concepts.body:
JSON Schema composition keywords:

- `allOf`: must match **all** subschemas. Used to extend a base schema (`allOf: [$ref Pet, {properties: {...}}]`).
- `oneOf`: must match **exactly one** subschema. Used for alternatives like payment methods.
- `anyOf`: must match **at least one**. Rarely what you want for typed SDKs.
- `not`: must not match.

`oneOf` is strict: if two alternatives both accept an object (e.g. neither forbids extra properties), the payload matches both and validation **fails**. Make variants mutually exclusive with `required` fields, `const` values or `additionalProperties: false`.

A **discriminator** names the property that tells variants apart, e.g. `type: card`. It is an OpenAPI addition (not JSON Schema) that helps code generators and validators choose the right class quickly. With `mapping` you connect values to schemas explicitly; otherwise the schema name is used. In 3.2, `defaultMapping` adds a fallback.

Give each variant a `const` for its discriminator value, so the document validates correctly even for tools that ignore `discriminator`.

Generated code quality varies a lot across generators with deep `allOf` chains, so keep composition shallow and test what your SDK generator produces.
concepts.code:
components:
  schemas:
    Payment:
      oneOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/CardPayment'
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/BankPayment'
      discriminator:
        propertyName: method
        mapping:
          card: '#/components/schemas/CardPayment'
          bank: '#/components/schemas/BankPayment'
    PaymentBase:
      type: object
      required: [method, amountCents]
      properties:
        amountCents: { type: integer, minimum: 1 }
    CardPayment:
      allOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/PaymentBase'
        - { type: object, required: [cardToken], properties: { method: { const: card }, cardToken: { type: string } } }
    BankPayment:
      allOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/PaymentBase'
        - { type: object, required: [iban], properties: { method: { const: bank }, iban: { type: string } } }
takeaways: allOf = all, oneOf = exactly one, anyOf = at least one
Make oneOf variants mutually exclusive or validation fails
A discriminator names the property that selects the variant
Use `const` on the discriminator property in each variant
pitfalls: oneOf variants that overlap, so valid payloads fail with 'matches more than one schema'.

quiz.q: A payload satisfies two schemas listed under `oneOf`. What is the result?
options: Invalid, it must match exactly one
quiz.explain: oneOf requires exactly one match; use exclusive variants.

concepts.name: Generating clients, servers and types
concepts.summary: Generate typed SDKs, server stubs or TypeScript types from an OpenAPI document, and decide between design-first and code-first.
concepts.why: Generated code removes a whole class of client/server mismatches.
concepts.body:
Code generation turns the contract into code, so client and server cannot silently disagree.

Common generators:

- **OpenAPI Generator** (community fork of Swagger Codegen): clients and server stubs for 50+ languages, highly configurable via templates.
- **openapi-typescript**: generates TypeScript types only; pair with the tiny `openapi-fetch` client for type-safe calls without heavy generated code.
- **Microsoft Kiota**, plus commercial SDK generators (Speakeasy, Stainless, Fern) for polished public SDKs.
- Language-specific options like `oapi-codegen` (Go) or `datamodel-code-generator` (Python Pydantic models).

**Code-first** frameworks generate the document from code: FastAPI from type hints, NestJS and Spring via annotations, `utoipa` in Rust. The code is the source of truth and the document is exported in CI.

**Design-first** writes the document first, reviews it as an API design artefact, mocks it, then generates server interfaces and clients.

Either way:

- Treat generated code as build output: regenerate in CI, do not hand-edit it.
- Pin generator versions; output changes between releases.
- Good `operationId`s, named component schemas and accurate `required` lists matter far more for SDK quality than any generator flag.
takeaways: Generate types, clients and stubs from the same contract
Code-first exports the document; design-first starts from it
Regenerate in CI and never hand-edit generated code
operationIds and named schemas make or break SDK quality
pitfalls: Hand-editing generated clients, then losing the edits on the next regeneration.

quiz.q: What mostly determines the readability of generated SDK method and type names?
quiz.explain: Generators derive method names from operationIds and type names from component names.

concepts.name: Linting, docs and mock servers
concepts.summary: Validate and lint documents with Redocly or Spectral, publish reference docs, and serve mocks with Prism.
concepts.why: Automated checks keep a growing API description consistent and useful.
concepts.body:
Three tool types belong in every OpenAPI workflow.

**Validation and linting.** Validation checks the document is legal OpenAPI. Linting enforces your style guide on top: every operation has an `operationId` and a `4XX` response, names are kebab-case paths and camelCase properties, no unused components, descriptions present.

- **Redocly CLI**: `redocly lint openapi.yaml` with configurable rules in `redocly.yaml`, plus `bundle` and `split` for multi-file documents.
- **Spectral** (Stoplight): rulesets written in YAML with JSONPath selectors; `spectral:oas` is the built-in set, and organisations publish their own.

Run linting in CI on every pull request that touches the API.

**Reference documentation.** Swagger UI, Redoc and Scalar render the document as browsable docs with request consoles. Descriptions support CommonMark Markdown, so write real explanations there, and use `tags` to structure the navigation.

**Mock servers.** **Prism** serves responses derived from your examples and schemas: `prism mock openapi.yaml`. Frontend and partner teams can build against the contract before the backend exists. Prism can also run as a **validation proxy** in front of a real server and report requests or responses that violate the contract.
concepts.code:
# Validate + lint with Redocly
npx @redocly/cli lint openapi.yaml
# validates the document and applies the recommended rules

# Bundle a multi-file description into one file for publishing
npx @redocly/cli bundle openapi.yaml -o dist/openapi.yaml

# Lint with Spectral (.spectral.yaml: extends: ["spectral:oas"])
npx @stoplight/spectral-cli lint openapi.yaml

# Mock server from examples and schemas
npx @stoplight/prism-cli mock openapi.yaml
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4010/books/123
# -> example (or generated) Book JSON

# Validation proxy in front of the real API
npx @stoplight/prism-cli proxy openapi.yaml http://localhost:8000
takeaways: Validate for correctness, lint for your style guide
Run lint in CI on every API change
Swagger UI, Redoc and Scalar render reference docs
Prism mocks the API and validates real traffic as a proxy
pitfalls: Mocks returning schema-generated junk because the document has no realistic examples.

quiz.q: What does Prism's proxy mode add when placed in front of a real API?
options: Reports of requests and responses that violate the contract
quiz.explain: As a proxy it forwards traffic and checks each exchange against the document.

concepts.name: Versioning and breaking-change detection
concepts.summary: Classify API changes as compatible or breaking, diff OpenAPI documents in CI, and plan versioning and deprecation.
concepts.why: Breaking a published API breaks other people's software; catching it in review is cheap.
concepts.body:
Because the document describes the whole contract, you can **diff** two versions mechanically. Tools like **oasdiff** compare the base branch document with the proposed one and classify each change.

Breaking for clients (typical list):

- Removing or renaming a path, operation, parameter, property or enum value in a response.
- Adding a **required** request parameter or required request property.
- Tightening constraints on requests (`maxLength` smaller, new `pattern`), or changing types.
- Making a response property optional or nullable that clients relied on.
- Changing security requirements or a successful status code.

Usually compatible: adding optional request fields, adding response fields (if clients ignore unknown fields), new operations, new optional parameters. Adding enum values to responses is a grey zone: strict clients and generated enums may break.

Strategy:

- Run the diff in CI and fail on breaking changes unless explicitly approved.
- Mark operations, parameters and schema properties `deprecated: true`, announce a sunset date (the `Sunset` and `Deprecation` HTTP headers help), and remove later.
- Choose a versioning scheme deliberately: URL major versions (`/v2`), a header, or date-based versions per request (Stripe style). Keep one OpenAPI document per supported version.
- Keep `info.version` meaningful and publish a changelog generated from the diffs.
concepts.code:
# Diff the PR's document against main and fail on breaking changes
git show origin/main:openapi.yaml > /tmp/base.yaml
oasdiff breaking /tmp/base.yaml openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR
# error [request-parameter-became-required] at openapi.yaml
#   in API GET /books
#     the 'query' request parameter 'genre' became required

# Human-readable changelog between versions
oasdiff changelog /tmp/base.yaml openapi.yaml

# Deprecate before removing
#   /books/{bookId}/legacy-cover:
#     get:
#       deprecated: true
#       description: Use /books/{bookId}/cover. Removed after 2027-01-31.
takeaways: Diff documents in CI and block unapproved breaking changes
Required inputs added or outputs removed are breaking
Deprecate with `deprecated: true` and a sunset date before removal
Pick one versioning scheme and keep a document per version
pitfalls: Assuming new response enum values are always safe; generated SDK enums may reject them.

quiz.q: Which change is breaking for existing clients?
options: Making an existing optional request property required
quiz.explain: Existing clients do not send the property, so their requests start failing.

concepts.name: Webhooks, callbacks, links and 3.2 additions
concepts.summary: Describe outgoing requests with webhooks and callbacks, connect operations with links, and know what OpenAPI 3.2 adds.
concepts.why: Event-driven and hypermedia-style APIs need more than request/response paths.
concepts.body:
OpenAPI can describe requests that **your API sends**:

- **Webhooks** (3.1+, top-level `webhooks`): named events your API POSTs to URLs that subscribers registered out of band. Each is a Path Item describing the request you send and the responses you expect.
- **Callbacks**: tied to a specific operation; the callback URL comes from the request at runtime via a **runtime expression** such as `'{$request.body#/callbackUrl}'`.

**Links** describe how a response value feeds another operation: after `createBook` returns `id`, the `GetBook` link says `bookId: $response.body#/id`. Tools can use links for navigation and test generation.

**OpenAPI 3.2** (September 2025) is backwards compatible with 3.1 and adds:

- Tags with `summary`, `parent` and `kind` for hierarchical navigation (replacing the `x-tagGroups` extension).
- The `QUERY` HTTP method, `additionalOperations` for other methods, and an `in: querystring` parameter for a whole query string described by one schema.
- Streaming and sequential media types (`text/event-stream`, `application/jsonl`, `application/json-seq`) with `itemSchema` describing each item.
- OAuth 2.0 device authorization flow, `oauth2MetadataUrl`, deprecating security schemes, and `defaultMapping` for discriminators.

Tool support for 3.2 is still catching up, so check your generators and validators before upgrading.

For purely asynchronous, broker-based APIs (Kafka, MQTT), the sibling **AsyncAPI** specification is the better fit.
concepts.code:
openapi: 3.1.1
info: { title: Orders API, version: 1.0.0 }
paths:
  /orders:
    post:
      operationId: createOrder
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Created
          links:
            GetOrder:
              operationId: getOrder
              parameters: { orderId: '$response.body#/id' }
  /orders/{orderId}:
    get:
      operationId: getOrder
      parameters:
        - { name: orderId, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string } }
      responses: { '200': { description: The order } }
webhooks:
  orderShipped:                 # we POST this to subscriber URLs
    post:
      requestBody:
        content: { application/json: { schema: { type: object, properties: { orderId: { type: string } } } } }
      responses: { '2XX': { description: Subscriber accepted the event } }
takeaways: Webhooks: events you send to registered URLs (3.1+)
Callbacks: per-operation, URL taken from the request at runtime
Links map response values to other operations' parameters
3.2 adds hierarchical tags, QUERY, streaming itemSchema
pitfalls: Describing webhooks as normal paths, which tells clients they can call them.

quiz.q: How does a callback differ from a webhook?
options: A callback's URL comes from a specific request at runtime; webhooks are registered separately
quiz.explain: Callbacks hang off an operation and use runtime expressions for their URL.

concepts.name: Contract testing against the document
concepts.summary: Prove the implementation matches the document with property-based API testing, runtime validation and consumer checks.
concepts.why: A description nobody tests drifts from reality, and every tool built on it inherits the lies.
concepts.body:
The contract is only useful if the running API honours it. Layers of defence:

**Schema-driven fuzzing.** **Schemathesis** reads the document and generates many requests (valid, edge-case and invalid) with property-based testing, then checks responses: status codes documented, bodies conform to schemas, no 5xx errors, content types right. It finds undocumented error responses and validation gaps quickly. Run it in CI against a test deployment.

**Runtime validation.** Middleware validates real requests (and optionally responses) against the document: `express-openapi-validator` for Express, `openapi-core` for Python, or built-in validation in code-first frameworks. Validating responses in staging catches drift as soon as it appears.

**Proxy validation.** Prism's proxy mode or API gateways check live traffic against the contract without code changes.

**Consumer-driven contracts.** Pact-style tests capture what each client actually uses; with bi-directional contract testing, consumer pacts are compared against the provider's OpenAPI document, so you know whether a change breaks a real consumer, not just a theoretical one.

Make the document honest first: realistic examples, complete error responses, `additionalProperties: false` where appropriate, and accurate `required` lists. Then test-driven drift checks become cheap and reliable.
concepts.code:
# Property-based testing of every operation
pip install schemathesis
st run ./openapi.yaml --url http://localhost:8000 \
  --checks all --max-examples 50 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_TOKEN"
# FAILED: POST /books
#   Undocumented HTTP status code: 500
#   Reproduce with: curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/books -d '{"title": ""}' ...

# Runtime validation middleware in an Express app:
#   import * as OpenApiValidator from "express-openapi-validator";
#   app.use(OpenApiValidator.middleware({
#     apiSpec: "./openapi.yaml",
#     validateRequests: true,
#     validateResponses: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
#   }));
takeaways: Fuzz the API from its schema with Schemathesis
Validate requests (and responses in staging) with middleware
Pair the provider contract with consumer-driven tests
Complete error responses and examples make tests meaningful
pitfalls: Generating the document from code and assuming it is therefore correct; annotations drift too.

quiz.q: What kind of problem does schema-driven fuzzing typically uncover?
options: Undocumented status codes and responses that violate schemas
quiz.explain: Generated edge-case inputs expose 5xx errors and responses that do not match the contract.
